title: WHAT IF THE SOULMATE YOU'VE BEEN PRAYING FOR IS A PROMISE GOD NEVER MADE?
paragraphs: WHAT IF THE SOULMATE YOU'VE BEEN PRAYING FOR IS A PROMISE GOD NEVER MADE?
The heartbreaking truth about “the one,” unanswered prayers, waiting for love, and why Jesus never promised you a perfect soulmate—but offered you something infinitely greater.
There is a prayer that has been whispered into pillows soaked with tears.
“Lord, where is my person?”
Not a stranger. Not just someone to hold hands with on Sunday. Not another relationship that begins with beautiful promises and ends with another broken piece of your heart.
Someone who stays.

Someone who understands your silence. Someone who sees the scars you have spent years hiding and doesn't turn away. Someone who chooses you when life becomes difficult, when beauty fades, when money runs out, when the excitement of falling in love becomes the ordinary responsibility of remaining faithful.
Maybe you've prayed for that person for years.
You've watched friends get engaged. You've attended weddings where you smiled for photographs, congratulated the newlyweds, and returned home to an apartment that suddenly felt painfully quiet.
You've heard testimonies about how God brought two people together.
And somewhere between another wedding invitation and another unanswered prayer, a frightening question entered your heart.
“God, did You forget about me?”
But what if the deepest problem isn't that God has failed to send your soulmate?
What if someone taught you to expect a promise that Scripture never actually made?
And what if believing that promise has quietly caused you to question God's goodness, overlook warning signs, idolize marriage, or measure your worth by whether someone chooses you?
Stay with me, because what the Bible actually says about love may disappoint the fantasy you've been carrying.
But it could also set your heart free.
The Bible never promises that every Christian will discover one perfect soulmate.
Read that again.
Not because marriage is unimportant. Not because romance is sinful. Not because your longing to be loved is foolish.
But because there is a difference between something God calls good and something God promises to give every believer.
And confusing those two things can leave a sincere Christian heartbroken over an expectation God never placed upon it.
Genesis 2:18 records the Lord saying:
“It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.” (KJV)
In the Hebrew text, the phrase translated “an help meet for him” is עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ — ʿezer kenegdô.
The word ʿezer means help or helper. It does not imply inferiority; the same Hebrew word is used elsewhere for the help God provides His people.
The expression kenegdô conveys the idea of someone corresponding to him, suitable for him, or standing as his counterpart.
God created Eve as a fitting partner for Adam.
This is a beautiful foundation for marriage.
But notice something essential.

Genesis 2 describes God's provision for the first man and establishes the goodness of human companionship and marriage. It does not declare that every person throughout history has one predetermined romantic counterpart whom they are guaranteed to find.
The passage gives us a theology of companionship.
It does not give us a universal promise of a soulmate.
And that distinction matters.
Because when you believe that God has promised you one perfect person, every failed relationship can begin to feel like a spiritual disaster.
Every rejection becomes a crisis of identity.
Every year of singleness becomes evidence that heaven is withholding something you were supposedly guaranteed.
You stop asking, “How can I faithfully follow Jesus in this season?”
And begin asking, “What is wrong with me that God hasn't given me what everyone else seems to have?”
That question can slowly poison your relationship with the very Savior who loves you.
But Scripture tells a different story.
Consider the apostle Paul.
Paul did not write about singleness as a shameful waiting room where incomplete Christians sit until marriage finally makes their lives meaningful.
He wrote:
“For I would that all men were even as I myself. But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that.” (1 Corinthians 7:7, KJV)
In the Greek text, the word translated “gift” is χάρισμα — charisma.
It refers to a gracious gift.
Paul recognized that believers receive different gifts and callings. He affirmed marriage as good while also recognizing the genuine value of remaining unmarried.
He continued:
“He that is unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please the Lord.” (1 Corinthians 7:32, KJV)
Paul was not declaring married Christians less spiritual.
He was explaining that unmarried believers can experience particular freedoms for undivided service to Christ.
Think about that.
A man whose writings helped shape Christian understanding for centuries did not teach that every believer must find a spouse to fulfill God's purpose.
And Jesus Himself lived an unmarried earthly life.
The sinless Son of God.
Perfect in obedience. Perfect in love. Perfect in His humanity.
Yet never married.
If marriage were necessary to become a complete human being, what would that imply about Jesus?
The thought itself exposes the weakness of the soulmate myth.
Marriage is a good gift, but it is not the measure of a complete life.
Jesus is.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that more than anything else tonight.
You are not half a person waiting for another half to arrive.
You are not spiritually defective because your wedding day hasn't come.
You are not less loved by God because nobody has placed a ring on your finger.
Your relationship status is not heaven's report card on your worth.
The cross has already revealed the immeasurable value of the grace God has extended to you.
But there is another side to this conversation, and it may be even more uncomfortable.
Some Christians are not merely waiting for a soulmate.
They are waiting for someone who will function like a savior.
Someone who will finally silence their insecurity.
Someone whose affection will erase childhood wounds.
Someone who will make them feel beautiful, chosen, protected, significant, and permanently safe.
And those desires often grow out of very real pain.
Maybe you grew up watching love disappear.
Maybe someone promised forever and abandoned you.
Maybe you were cheated on, manipulated, humiliated, or made to believe you were difficult to love.
So now you dream of meeting someone whose love will undo everything another person destroyed.
But even a faithful spouse cannot carry the weight of being your redeemer.
A husband cannot forgive your sins.
A wife cannot reconcile your soul to God.
A romantic relationship cannot provide the ultimate security that belongs to Christ alone.
Human love is precious.
But human love was never designed to replace divine love.
This is why Colossians 2:10 is so important:
“And ye are complete in him, which is the head of all principality and power.” (KJV)
The Greek expression is ἐστὲ ἐν αὐτῷ πεπληρωμένοι — este en autō peplērōmenoi.
In context, Paul is declaring the spiritual fullness believers possess in Christ, not promising that Christians will never experience loneliness or emotional need.
That matters.
Being complete in Christ does not mean you never desire marriage.
It means marriage is not the source of your standing before God.
You can long for a spouse without making that spouse your god.
You can pray for companionship without treating singleness as a curse.
You can grieve a broken relationship without believing your future has been destroyed.
And you can be deeply loved by Jesus while still experiencing the very human ache of an empty chair beside you.
Faith does not require pretending loneliness never hurts.
Sometimes the most faithful prayer is simply:
“Lord, I trust You. But this is hard.”
And God is not offended by honest lament.
The Psalms are filled with people bringing their anguish before Him.
You do not have to disguise your tears to qualify for His compassion.
Now consider another phrase Christians often repeat:
“When you meet the one, you'll just know.”
Really?
Where does Scripture promise that?

The Bible certainly describes remarkable marriages and providential encounters. Isaac and Rebekah's story in Genesis 24 is one example of God's guidance within a particular family and covenant history.
But a descriptive biblical narrative is not automatically a promise that every Christian will experience the same circumstances.
Ruth and Boaz also have a beautiful story.
Yet Ruth's account includes widowhood, poverty, courage, loyalty, and difficult decisions. It is not simply a romantic formula for obtaining a spouse.
And neither story teaches that a person should ignore wisdom, character, or warning signs because a relationship feels destined.
In fact, one of the most dangerous consequences of the soulmate myth is how easily it can be used to excuse unhealthy relationships.
“He's my soulmate, so I have to endure whatever he does.”
“God showed me she's the one, so the warning signs don't matter.”
“We have such a powerful spiritual connection. Surely that means we're supposed to be together.”
But intensity is not the same as intimacy.
Chemistry is not character.
And a strong feeling is not automatically the voice of the Holy Spirit.
A person may know how to speak Christian language while refusing to practice Christian love.
They may quote Scripture while manipulating your conscience.
They may pray beautifully in public while treating you cruelly in private.
Please hear this.
God does not require you to surrender biblical wisdom in order to prove your faith in a romantic relationship.
First Corinthians 13:4–5 says:

“Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil.” (KJV)
The Greek word translated “charity” is ἀγάπη — agapē.
It means love, and in this passage Paul describes the character and conduct of love.

This passage is not exclusively about marriage. Its original context concerns love within the Christian community. Nevertheless, its teaching provides a powerful standard for how Christians should treat one another, including within marriage.
Love is patient.
Love is kind.
Love does not rejoice in wrongdoing.
And love does not become godly merely because someone attaches the phrase “God told me” to it.
If someone continually humiliates you, controls you, threatens you, or uses Scripture to silence you, do not confuse that behavior with biblical love.
Forgiveness is Christian.
But forgiveness does not require remaining in danger, pretending abuse is acceptable, or restoring trust without repentance and meaningful change.
The Gospel calls sinners to repentance.
It does not call victims to sanctify cruelty.
And perhaps that is the freedom someone needs today.
Not the freedom to find a soulmate.
But the freedom to stop calling a destructive relationship God's will.
Because sometimes the relationship you're afraid to lose is the very relationship that has taught you to forget who you are in Christ.
And still, Scripture does not ask us to become cynical about marriage.
Marriage is beautiful.
It is God's creation, not humanity's invention.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.” (KJV)
The Hebrew phrase בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar ʾeḥad means “one flesh.”
This is covenantal union, not a claim that two people were previously incomplete fragments of one soul.
And in Ephesians 5:31–32, Paul connects marriage to a profound mystery concerning Christ and the Church.
Christian marriage is meant to reflect something beyond romantic fulfillment.
It points toward covenant faithfulness, sacrificial love, and the relationship between Christ and His people.
That means the most important question in choosing a spouse is not simply:
“Does this person give me butterflies?”
But also:
“Can we honor Christ together?”
“Is there honesty when nobody is watching?”
“Does this person demonstrate humility and repentance?”
“Are we willing to forgive, serve, grow, and remain faithful through ordinary and difficult seasons?”
“Are we both pursuing Jesus rather than expecting each other to become Jesus?”
The Bible gives us principles for wise and godly relationships, not a guaranteed method for identifying one flawless romantic destiny.
And here is another truth that may challenge what you've been taught.
Even if you marry a wonderful Christian, you will not marry a perfect person.
Two redeemed sinners can build a beautiful covenant.
But they will still need grace.
There will be misunderstandings.
Exhausting days.
Unspoken expectations.
Disagreements about money.
Moments when affection feels easier than patience.
Seasons when love looks less like a romantic movie and more like choosing kindness when both people are tired.
A healthy marriage is not the discovery of someone who never disappoints you.
It is the faithful cultivation of covenant love between imperfect people who continue to need God's mercy.
And this is why the fantasy of a perfect soulmate can actually damage a good marriage.
If you believe your spouse was created to satisfy every emotional longing, normal disappointments may begin to feel like proof that you married the wrong person.
But perhaps you did not marry the wrong person.
Perhaps you married a human being.
Someone who needs the same grace you do.
Someone who cannot read your mind.
Someone whose sanctification, like yours, is still unfolding.
Christian marriage is not sustained by perfection.
It requires faithfulness, repentance, forgiveness, wisdom, and the continuing grace of God.

That does not mean every marriage is healthy or that every broken marriage can be repaired by one person's effort. Scripture recognizes serious covenant violations, and situations involving abuse require safety and wise intervention.
But it does mean that ordinary imperfection is not evidence that love has failed.
Sometimes real love begins to mature precisely when fantasy ends.
And now we come to a question that has broken many hearts.
“What if I never get married?”
Not everyone will.
Scripture does not hide that possibility.
In Matthew 19:12, Jesus speaks about those who remain unmarried for different reasons, including those who choose celibacy for the kingdom of heaven.
In 1 Corinthians 7, Paul explicitly recognizes both marriage and singleness within Christian life.
There is no biblical promise that every believer who prays faithfully, waits patiently, and maintains sexual purity will eventually receive a spouse.
Purity is not a payment for marriage.
Prayer is not a transaction.
Obedience is not a vending machine where you insert faithfulness and receive a wedding ring.
And God is not indebted to us because we have waited.
That may be painful to hear.
Especially if you have been told, “Just keep believing. Your husband is coming.”
Or, “God wouldn't put the desire for marriage in your heart unless He planned to fulfill it.”
Those statements may be intended as encouragement.
But neither is a universal promise found in Scripture.
Psalm 37:4 says:
“Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart.” (KJV)
Yet this verse belongs to a psalm about trusting God, refusing envy, committing one's way to Him, and waiting faithfully amid injustice.
It is not a blank check guaranteeing every personal desire exactly as imagined.
Delighting in the Lord changes our relationship with our desires. It does not make God a servant of our preferred timeline.
And Jeremiah 29:11, so often quoted as proof that a desired marriage must be coming, was originally spoken to God's people in exile concerning His purposes for their future restoration.
Its original context must not be erased to turn it into a personalized guarantee of romance.
God is faithful.
But we honor His faithfulness by trusting what He has actually promised.
Not by inventing promises and becoming angry when they are not fulfilled.
So what has He promised?
Jesus said:
“I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.” (Hebrews 13:5, KJV)
Romans 8:38–39 declares that nothing in all creation can separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
And John 6:37 records Jesus saying:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (KJV)
These promises are not small consolation prizes for people who never find romantic love.
They are the foundation of eternal hope.
A spouse may walk beside you for decades.
Christ is your Savior forever.
A marriage may be a beautiful earthly covenant.
But the Gospel offers reconciliation with God Himself.
And this is where the story becomes even more astonishing.
Because the Bible does contain a love story greater than the search for a soulmate.
It is the story of a holy God pursuing sinners through the saving work of His Son.
Not because we were flawless.
Not because we were desirable by worldly standards.
Not because we had earned His affection.
But because of His mercy and grace.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
The Greek word συνίστησιν — synistēsin, translated here as “commendeth,” carries the sense of demonstrating or showing.
God demonstrates His love through Christ's death for sinners.
This is not romantic love.
It is something infinitely more consequential.
It is redemptive love.
Love that confronts sin rather than pretending it does not exist.
Love that does not abandon justice but satisfies it through the saving work of Jesus Christ.
Love that calls us to repentance, faith, and new life.
And perhaps this is the most important correction we can make to the soulmate narrative.
The greatest love story in Scripture is not about finding the perfect person. It is about the perfect Savior redeeming imperfect people.
You may have a scandal in your past.
A relationship you regret.
A sexual sin you have tried to bury.
A divorce that still hurts.
A betrayal that left you questioning whether love can ever be trusted again.
Perhaps you stayed where you should have left.
Perhaps you wounded someone who trusted you.
Perhaps you crossed boundaries you once promised yourself you would never cross.
And now shame whispers:
“Who would want someone like you?”
But shame does not get the final word over a repentant sinner who comes to Jesus.
The cross does.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
And 2 Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” (KJV)
This does not erase every earthly consequence of our choices.
But it does announce the extraordinary reality of new life in Christ.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It does not have authority to cancel the grace of God.
And the person who has been rejected by people can still be welcomed by Christ.
The person who has sinned can repent and be forgiven.
The person who has been abandoned can still discover that the Lord is near to the brokenhearted.
The person who never marries can still live a life overflowing with purpose, friendship, service, holiness, and joy.
Because from scandal to grace is not merely the story of a broken romance becoming a happy marriage.
It is the story of a sinner being brought from death to life through Jesus Christ.
And that story does not require a wedding ring.
It requires a Savior.
Maybe you will marry someday.
Maybe the person God providentially brings into your life will be someone whose faithfulness, humility, kindness, and love make you thank Him every morning.
If so, receive that gift with gratitude.
But do not worship the gift.
Maybe you are already married and have spent years comparing your spouse to an imaginary perfect person.
If so, perhaps today is the day to repent of unrealistic expectations and begin practicing the patient, truthful, sacrificial love Scripture commands.
And maybe you are single, tired, and frightened that the years are passing too quickly.
You do not need another shallow assurance that your wedding is just around the corner.
You need something stronger than a prediction.
You need truth sturdy enough to hold you even if your circumstances do not change.
Here it is.
God's goodness is not measured by whether you get married.
Christ's sufficiency is not disproved by your loneliness.
And your usefulness in the kingdom of God is not postponed until someone chooses you.
You can serve now.
Grow now.
Love your neighbors now.
Build meaningful friendships now.
Pursue holiness now.
Participate in the life of the Church now.
Seek wise counsel, develop character, and remain open to marriage if that is your desire.
You do not have to choose between contentment and hope.
You can desire marriage deeply while refusing to make it the condition of your joy in Christ.
You can pray boldly without pretending you know God's answer.
And you can grieve honestly without surrendering your trust in Him.

There is a profound difference between saying, “Jesus, I will follow You once You give me the person I want,” and saying, “Jesus, I will follow You because You are worthy, whether or not that person ever comes.”
The second prayer is not easy.
Sometimes it must be prayed through tears.
But it is the prayer of a heart learning that Jesus is not merely the means to a better life.
He is life itself.
And one day, earthly marriage will no longer be the center of anyone's hope.
Jesus teaches in Matthew 22:30 that in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage.
And Revelation 19:7–9 presents the glorious imagery of the marriage supper of the Lamb.
The ultimate fulfillment toward which Christian marriage points is not an endless earthly romance.
It is the consummation of Christ's relationship with His redeemed people.
The Church is described as the bride of Christ.
Not because Jesus is a romantic replacement for a human spouse, but because Scripture uses covenant marriage imagery to reveal His faithful, saving love for His people.
That is the greater story.
And it changes how we understand every lesser love.
So tonight, if you are still waiting, I want to leave you with something more valuable than the promise of a soulmate.
You are invited to trust a Savior who has already given Himself for sinners.
You are invited to surrender your fears, desires, regrets, and future to Him.
You are invited to stop measuring your life against engagement announcements and wedding photographs.
You are invited to believe that the God who raised Jesus from the dead is not powerless to sustain you in a season you never expected.
And if you have made romance an idol, you can repent.
If you have made marriage the condition of your obedience, you can surrender.
If you have placed unbearable expectations upon another human being, you can ask God to reshape your understanding of love.
If you have believed your singleness makes you worthless, you can reject that lie in light of the Gospel.
Not because everything will suddenly become easy.
But because Jesus Christ is worthy of your trust even in the unanswered places.
Perhaps the most courageous thing you will do after reading this is not download another dating app, search for another sign, or beg God to reveal the name of your future spouse.
Perhaps it will be to sit quietly before Him and say:

“Lord Jesus, I still desire to be loved by someone. I still hope for marriage. I still struggle when I see other people receiving what I have prayed for. But forgive me for treating a relationship as though it could save me. Teach me to seek You first. Give me wisdom if marriage comes, contentment and faithful purpose in every season, and courage to trust You with what I cannot control. Heal what has been wounded. Expose what needs repentance. And make my life a testimony of Your grace, whether I walk through it married or single. Amen.”
And if that prayer touched a place you have kept hidden, please don't feel pressured to pretend you're fine.
You don't need to reveal private details. Even a few honest words can open the door for another believer to encourage you, pray with you, and remind you that you are not alone in the body of Christ.

And if you are married, consider sharing what God has taught you about the difference between romantic expectations and faithful covenant love. Your testimony may help someone entering marriage with unrealistic expectations.
Not everyone who needs it will admit they are struggling.
Someone scrolling tonight may be questioning God's goodness because another relationship ended.
Someone may be preparing to marry a person whose character they have ignored because they believe they have found their destined soulmate.
Someone may be quietly wondering whether their unmarried life has any purpose at all.

Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, those wrestling with their faith, and even those who do not yet know Christ to follow along. The Gospel is too important to keep confined to people who already agree with us.
There is also another way you can help this ministry continue.
Rather, it is one voluntary way to glorify Him through generosity by helping support the creation, continuation, and expansion of Gospel-centered teaching and discipleship resources.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, not coerced:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV)
Monthly supporters help sustain this work and make it possible to reach more people with biblical teaching, encouragement, and resources rooted in the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
We want the truth of Scripture to remain accessible, because the grace of God is not for sale.
The goal has never been merely to grow a page.
It is to see people come to know Jesus, turn from sin, receive His grace, grow in His Word, and walk faithfully with Him.
That is what matters.
And before you leave, remember the question that brought you here.
Does the Bible promise that every Christian will discover a perfect soulmate?
No.
But it reveals something far greater than the soulmate fantasy.
A perfect Savior who receives repentant sinners.
A faithful Lord who never abandons His people.
A Redeemer whose love is not dependent on your relationship status.
A King whose kingdom gives purpose to both marriage and singleness.
And a Gospel powerful enough to transform even the most painful chapters of your story.
You may never know what tomorrow will bring.
You may still desire marriage.
You may still cry over what has not happened.
But you do not have to wait for another human being to make your life worth living.
Because your deepest need was never a perfect soulmate.
It was reconciliation with God.
And Jesus Christ came to accomplish what no human relationship ever could.
You may spend years waiting for someone to choose you, but never let that waiting blind you to the Savior who gave His life to redeem you.
